name: High-trust / low-trust face

card.summary: A looksmaxxing framework that says faces read as trustworthy or untrustworthy at a glance, so softening trust-related cues (eyes, brows, expression, skin, grooming) can improve how someone is perceived beyond bone structure alone.
card.aka: high trust face, low trust face, high trust, low trust
card.note: The forum framework is informal; the underlying face-perception research measures first impressions, not character.

quick.overview:
High-trust and low-trust are labels used on looksmax.org for how trustworthy, approachable and non-threatening a face looks on first sight. A high-trust face is described as warm and open; a low-trust face as cold, hostile or intimidating. Proponents argue that this impression can matter as much as, or more than, raw bone structure for how others respond to someone.

The idea parallels psychology research on first impressions, in which people rapidly judge trustworthiness and dominance from faces, and in which cues such as resting expression and brow and mouth shape shift those judgments. The research measures what viewers perceive; it does not show those perceptions are accurate.
quick.how: Community members post photos and ask whether their face reads high-trust or low-trust. Suggested adjustments discussed include relaxed or slightly upturned resting expression, eye and brow presentation, grooming, skin clarity and hairstyle, with threads on how to look more high-trust.
quick.risks: The framework is an informal community construct and the labels are subjective. Threads often treat the labels as fixed verdicts, which researchers on first impressions caution against, since face-based judgments are fast but weak predictors of actual character. Surgical or cosmetic changes pursued for this goal carry their ordinary risks.

lead: High-trust / low-trust face is a framework used in looksmaxxing communities, especially looksmax.org, for how trustworthy and approachable a face appears at first glance. A high-trust face is described as friendly, open and non-threatening, while a low-trust face is described as cold, severe or menacing [2][3]. The framework is used to explain why two people with similar attractiveness ratings can receive different reactions from others.

For appearance, the idea points to features that are often adjustable: resting expression, brow position, eye area, skin and grooming. Members post photos and ask for classification, and discuss how to look more high-trust [4]. Some threads argue the distinction is overstated or misapplied, and others ask whether it is a real phenomenon at all [5].

The terms echo academic work on first impressions. Psychologist Alexander Todorov and colleagues have studied how observers infer traits such as trustworthiness and dominance from faces within a fraction of a second, and how these inferences correlate with real-world outcomes such as election results [1]. The forum framework is informal and not drawn directly from this literature.

chain: Face cues (resting expression, brows, eyes, skin, grooming) shape the first impression
Viewers read the face as warmer or colder within a moment
Others respond with more or less openness
angle.text: Practitioners look at the cues that make a face read as warm or threatening and adjust the changeable ones: expression, grooming, hairstyle and skin. The aim is to be received as approachable rather than to change bone structure.

infobox: Faces read as high-trust (warm, safe) or low-trust (cold, threatening)
Social attributions from faces (Todorov and colleagues)

paras: In forum usage a high-trust face is one that looks gentle, kind or safe, often associated by posters with soft or upturned eye and mouth shape, relaxed brows and a neutral-to-pleasant resting expression. A low-trust face is one posters describe as hard, brooding or predatory, for example with a heavy brow, deep-set or downturned eyes or a severe resting expression [2][3].

Threads range from rating requests such as asking whether specific eyes are low-trust or high-trust [6][7] to broader arguments that the quality decides how people are treated socially [8]. Several posters describe a personal shift between the two categories after changes in weight, grooming or expression [9].

The terms circulate in looksmax.org's face-analysis culture alongside concepts such as the blackpill, and appear in threads going back several years [10]. Posters have also written about how they came to adopt the idea [11]. The framework is a community construct; no single originator is documented.

Proponents say trust impressions form instantly, strongly affect social and dating treatment, and are partly independent of attractiveness. Skeptics within the same community argue that the labels are used loosely, that it is hard to tell which features drive them, or that it is an unfalsifiable explanation [5].

Psychologists studying face perception find that observers form trait impressions such as trustworthiness from faces almost immediately, and agree with one another to a notable degree [1]. Todorov's work, summarised in his 2017 book Face Value, argues that these impressions are consequential but are poor guides to actual character [1].

Experimental stimuli in this field are typically computer-generated faces varied along trustworthiness dimensions, in which smiling-like and emotion-resembling features raise ratings. The forum framework applies the idea to real faces and bone structure, which this research does not directly test.
No studies found. Related academic work on social attributions from faces is described under Research and expert views [1].

timeline.event: Todorov and colleagues report that inferences of competence from faces predict election outcomes [1].
Todorov publishes Face Value: The Irresistible Influence of First Impressions [1].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, high-trust and low-trust are used both as descriptive tags and as claims about social outcomes [2][3].

claims.claim: A face's trust impression matters as much as bone structure
claims.believers: Posters argue that being read as safe or threatening drives how people treat you and say it explains differences between similarly rated faces [8].
claims.experts: Research shows trait impressions from faces form quickly and affect some decisions, though they are weak predictors of real traits [1].

claims.claim: You can look more high-trust by changing expression, grooming and eye-area presentation
claims.believers: Members share tips and before/after photos in threads on how to look more high-trust [4].
claims.experts: Studies of face perception find expression-related cues shift trustworthiness ratings; no trial has tested the forum's specific recommendations [1].

claims.claim: High-trust vs low-trust is a real, useful distinction
claims.believers: Many posters sort faces into the two groups and treat it as obvious [2].
claims.experts: Academic researchers describe trustworthiness impressions as a continuum measured by viewer ratings rather than two categories [1]. Some forum members also question whether the idea is real [5].
